c0617: Zoning check before signing: restaurant use, hood, seats and patio
c0620: Ask the city planning (zoning) office whether the zoning allows a restaurant with a flat-top griddle, trompos and a fryer, whether the space can take a Type I hood with a duct up to the roof, what occupancy load it allows, and whether the city permits patio seating on that street. Then ask the fire marshal in writing what the hood and fire suppression requirements are. With no exhaust path to the roof, there are no trompos, griddle or comal.
c0621: Decide gas or charcoal trompo BEFORE signing the lease (charcoal = solid fuel: separate exhaust, NFPA 96)
c0623: A gas trompo (the plan's case) works with a standard Type I hood, installed by a licensed gas contractor. A charcoal trompo, like a charcoal carne asada grill, is a solid-fuel appliance under NFPA 96: it needs a separate exhaust, a spark arrestor and daily ash removal. Ask the fire marshal in writing whether your space can take it.
c0624: Decide whether to buy tortillas or make your own BEFORE signing the lease
c0625: The plan buys its tortillas. Making them in-house takes a masa harina mixer or nixtamal mill, a tortilla machine or press, kitchen space and a dedicated tortilla maker; on cost alone it only pays off above about 656 tortillas a day (the Taco Cost & Trompo Yield Calculator in the kit runs the math with your prices). If you make them yourself, the equipment has to fit in the space.
c0634: Business license + sales tax permit (state and city)
c0636: Register with your state revenue department for a sales tax permit and with your city or county for a business license. Some states also ask for a separate food seller or retail license. Rules, fees and timing vary by state, so confirm them with your CPA before you open and collect sales tax from your first sale.
c0647: Bring the complete financial plan, with the month-by-month cash flow. Ask for quotes on equipment leasing for the walk-in cooler and the kitchen line, and ask each lender about the SBA Microloan (up to $50,000) as a complement. Lenders usually expect an owner equity injection (often around 10% for SBA start-ups; many want 20-30%).
c0651: Get quotes for general liability, liquor liability (if you will serve beer and wine), property and workers' comp. Tell the broker you cook on gas with trompos, a griddle and a fryer, and ask about equipment breakdown and spoilage coverage for the walk-in cooler.
c0654: Use the dropdown: ✓, ☐, N/A. ✓ = done, ☐ = pending, N/A = not applicable and comes out of the total.
c0657: Choose the space: about 1,200 sq ft (111 sq m), second-generation if you can, with a possible hood and duct route to the roof
c0659: Dining area of about 480 sq ft (45 sq m) for 30 seats at the counter and tables, an open kitchen of about 215 sq ft (20 sq m) with the trompos in view, restrooms (one ADA-accessible) and storage; the patio adds 12 seats from April to October. Look for a street with foot traffic in the evenings and on weekends, near a campus or an entertainment district.
c0660: Check the electrical service and the gas capacity
c0663: Refrigeration, hood fans and makeup air, HVAC and the dish machine run on electric; trompos, griddle, comal and burners run on gas (natural gas or propane). A new gas service takes time: ask the utility for the lead time and the cost.
c0664: Confirm the hood and duct route to the roof with your mechanical contractor
c0668: The plan counts two months of rent before opening and a two-month security deposit. Ask for free rent while the build-out and the hood and duct are under way.
c0669: Lease with restaurant use, hood rights and a beer & wine license contingency
c0672: It should say "restaurant" (or "taqueria with a kitchen"), approve the hood and duct work up to the roof, and be contingent on getting your beer & wine license if you plan to serve it.
c0673: Commission architect and MEP drawings, including the hood and duct
c0676: Kitchen layout, electrical load, occupancy, ventilation, ADA accessibility, the gas line and the duct to the roof. Ask your city or county for its mechanical and fire code requirements for commercial kitchens.
c0679: Restaurants go through your city's own process: zoning approval first, then a certificate of occupancy after the final inspections. Ask the planning office which permits apply to your address and in what order.
c0680: Building permit for the build-out and the hood
c0682: The build-out and the hood run through their own building permit and inspections: ask the building department which drawings and sign-offs they require.
c0686: Sidewalk and patio seating needs its own city permit, always applied for separately. Ask about the fee, the hours and the insurance requirements; the plan includes an example fee.
c0687: Licensed gas contractor + permit and inspection
c0690: Gas permit and inspection, plus start-up and testing of the trompos, griddle, comal and burners by the licensed contractor. Keep the inspection sign-off in your permit file and ask the contractor about periodic gas appliance service.
c0691: Type I hood, UL 300 suppression and makeup air (charcoal: solid-fuel rules)
c0694: The hood and duct need a mechanical permit: check your local code for the duct route and where the exhaust discharges. A gas trompo (the plan's case) uses a standard Type I system; charcoal or any other solid fuel adds NFPA 96 requirements (separate exhaust, spark arrestor, daily ash removal). Ask the fire marshal in writing.
c0695: Kitchen and dining area build-out: smooth, washable surfaces
c0700: Hot and cold water in the kitchen, drains with a grease interceptor (the griddle and the fryer send a lot of grease down the line) and HVAC for the dining area. Check your sewer authority's rules.
c0701: Fire marshal sign-off of the hood and suppression system, plus a Class K extinguisher
c0703: Type I hood over the trompos, griddle, comal and fryer, with grease filters, a UL 300 fire suppression system and makeup air. Ask the installer for the airflow figures and the filter cleaning schedule. The fire marshal inspects and signs off; keep a Class K extinguisher within reach of the fryer.
c0704: Final inspections and certificate of occupancy
c0707: The final sign-offs (electrical, gas, mechanical, fire and building) and the certificate of occupancy. Keep them together with the gas paperwork: your health department and your insurer may ask for them.
c0710: Buy the trompos, flat-top griddle, comal and fryer
c0711: Gas vertical broilers (trompos), three- or four-burner models sized for the cones you will run (the plan's case uses 30 lb (13.6 kg) cones), a flat-top griddle, a comal and a fryer. Compare data sheets and prices from at least two restaurant-supply dealers, and ask for the gas load, delivery time and installation.
c0712: Buy refrigeration: walk-in cooler, freezer and refrigerated salsa prep table
c0714: Space for the marinated meat and the stacked cones, a freezer, and a refrigerated prep table that holds the salsas and salsa bar toppings at 41 °F (5 °C) or below.
c0718: Submit your plans for plan review (Food Code 8-201.11) before construction, then apply for the health permit and book the pre-opening inspection. Requirements, fees and timing are set by your county or state. If you plan to sell tortillas or masa to other businesses, ask about wholesale food rules too.
c0719: Marinated cones held at 41 °F (5 °C) or below, date-marked
c0722: Marinated al pastor meat is a TCS food: keep it in the walk-in cooler at 41 °F (5 °C) or below. Log the marinating time and the stacking time of each cone and date-mark it.
c0723: Get your county's vertical broiler rules in writing (cook temp, max time on the broiler, leftover cone) and write your trompo SOP
c0725: Counties differ: some use 145 °F (63 °C) and others 155 °F (68 °C) for pork on a vertical broiler, and chicken is 165 °F (74 °C). Take no figure as the rule until your health department confirms it. Probe at the start and midway through service, slice only the outer layer that has reached temperature, and put the maximum time a cone may stay on the broiler in your SOP.
c0726: Cut tomatoes, fresh salsas and guacamole at 41 °F (5 °C) or below
c0728: Cut tomatoes are a TCS food, so pico de gallo and fresh salsas stay at 41 °F (5 °C) or below. Guacamole: treat it as TCS and ask your regulator. Prep in small batches. Avocado browning is a quality issue, not a safety one: use lime juice and film pressed on the surface.
c0729: Carnitas and guisados: hot holding, cooling and reheating
c0730: Hot holding at 135 °F (57 °C) or above. Cool what you store with a written procedure that follows the Food Code cooling steps, and reheat to 165 °F (74 °C) within 2 hours. Log the temperatures.
c0731: Salsa bar: cold holding or TPHC with a written procedure, labels and utensils
c0733: Clean container at every refill (never top off), put-out and discard times logged, and a separate utensil for each salsa. If you use time as a public health control (Food Code 3-501.19: 4 or 6 hours), you need a written procedure. Salsa macha gets its own spoon because it contains peanuts and sesame.
c0734: Ceviche or aguachile: parasite destruction by freezing or a supplier letter
c0735: If it is on the menu
c0736: Freeze the fish at the times and temperatures in Food Code 3-402.11 (ask your health department), or buy fish that arrives already frozen with a written supplier guarantee. Keep the record on file.
c0737: Cheese, crema and packaged tortillas held at the temperature on the label
c0738: Dairy such as queso fresco and crema is TCS: hold it at 41 °F (5 °C) or below. Anything else goes at the temperature the manufacturer's label sets.
c0739: Traceability and records: lots, temperatures and suppliers
c0741: Lot and date of the meat, tortillas and cheeses, the marinating and stacking time of each cone, cold and hot holding temperatures, and the supplier of each ingredient.
c0742: Recipe cards for each taco and salsa, with their allergens
c0743: Wheat (the flour tortilla on the gringa, beer), milk (cheeses, crema), peanuts and sesame (salsa macha, moles), tree nuts (moles) and others depending on the recipe. Corn tortillas are naturally gluten-free, but a shared comal and fryer mean you never promise it. Cost each recipe with the Taco Cost & Trompo Yield Calculator.
c0746: Allergen information has to be available before the guest orders online or through a marketplace. Check the listing of each taco on every marketplace and on your own website, and keep them in sync with your allergen cards.
c0749: Packaging that holds temperature in transit (hot at 135 °F (57 °C) or above, cold at 41 °F (5 °C) or below), also on marketplace deliveries. Pack in clamshells, foil and salsa cups, and check local packaging rules. Build-your-own orders (tortillas and filling packed separately) arrive better.
c0754: Set pay rates against the state and local minimum wage and post the required labor law posters. Enter the state or local minimum wage in the "0. Assumptions" tab: payroll is hourly W-2, with overtime under FLSA and your state's rules.
c0757: Hire the second taquero before opening
c0758: Have them learn the marinade, the cone stacking and the slicing with you before opening: if only you can run the trompo, one sick day closes the shop.
c0761: Keep hours for every employee, part-time included (FLSA recordkeeping). A time clock in the POS makes it simple; agree with your CPA how to store the records.
c0769: Training is the employer's job (there is no single official document to pull): hygiene, trompo and salsa temperatures, allergens and cross-contact. Get a CFPM certificate for the person in charge and food handler cards as your state requires.
c0770: Trompo training: marinade, cone stacking and slicing
c0771: Adobo, layers, pineapple, lighting the burners, thin slicing of the cooked outer layer and portion size per taco: this is an investment, not an expense.
c0774: Cover cuts from the trompo knife, burns from the griddle and the fryer, gas, heat and lifting. Write a short safety plan and train the team on it (OSHA basics).
c0778: Allergen information on the menu or by staff script, with a written record
c0779: In writing on the menu or, if staff give it verbally, backed by a written record kept on site and a sign telling guests to ask. Keep one allergen matrix up to date for the whole menu.
c0780: Allergen signs at the salsa bar
c0781: Each salsa with its allergens in plain view of the guest: salsa macha contains peanuts and sesame. Review the signs every time a recipe changes.
c0782: Never promise a gluten claim with a shared comal or fryer
c0784: Corn tortillas are naturally gluten-free, but a comal, fryer or tongs shared with the flour tortillas break any promise (FDA rule 21 CFR 101.91 allows the claim only under 20 ppm). Say it this way: "corn tortillas are naturally gluten-free; ask about our fryer and griddle". Disclose the allergen and the cross-contact risk instead of promising.
c0787: Decide the type of taqueria and its menu
c0789: A neighborhood taco shop without a trompo, with a trompo and a salsa bar (this plan), with its own tortilleria, or a taqueria-cantina that needs a full liquor license: each takes different capital, space and margin. A sit-down Mexican restaurant with a full bar is a different business; this kit is for counter service with beer & wine only.
c0790: A menu of 8-10 tacos, with taco costing
c0792: Cost every taco, the order of 3 and the gringa, not only the al pastor: carnitas, suadero and barbacoa yield less and avocado prices swing. Use the Taco Cost & Trompo Yield Calculator in the kit.
c0793: Sales tax on the menu: one rate in the example; check your state's to-go rules
c0795: The plan uses a single example sales tax rate on all sales. Some states tax to-go food, soft drinks and alcohol differently: ask your CPA and set up each rate in the POS and on every marketplace.
c0799: Many cities and states ban foam and single-use plastic or charge a fee for bags and containers. Check your city's packaging ordinance before you order to-go containers, and ask your supplier for compliant options.
c0800: Mexican specialty distributor (dried chiles, masa harina) + a backup
c0801: Dried chiles, achiote, masa harina and imported products can take weeks to arrive: get lead times in writing, hold safety stock and sign a second distributor. This is the real bottleneck of the business.
c0802: Tortilla supplier: lot, receiving temperature and a second supplier
c0803: Corn tortillas (nixtamalized) with lot and date, received at the temperature on the label and logged. Ask two manufacturers for samples and a price per case. The plan uses 6 in (15 cm) tortillas at a reference price, 360 per case: enter your own.
c0805: Read the commission (tiers vary by plan and zone on DoorDash, Uber Eats and Grubhub), how often they pay out, who pays for promotions and what the tablet costs. Set a ceiling on the share of your sales you will let marketplaces take, and write it down.
c0807: Calculate the margin of the order of 3 and the gringa on the marketplace, with its commission and the packaging. Pickup at the shop pays no commission: push it.
c0810: Run a trademark search first to make sure the name is not registered in your class (restaurant services), and check your state's business name registry.
c0811: Brand identity, photos and website with the menu and allergens
c0814: Real photos of the trompo and the tacos; a website with the menu, allergens, hours, pickup ordering and a privacy policy for each channel.
c0815: Google Business Profile, social media and Mexican holidays
c0816: Lunch and dinner hours, photos of the trompo and a reply to every review. On the calendar: Cinco de Mayo, Mexican Independence Day (September 15-16) and Day of the Dead (November 1-2).
c0821: Open in January, Month 1 of the plan
c0823: The plan starts in January and the ramp-up falls on the slowest months, January and February: that is why working capital matters. If you open in another month, rotate the seasonality row of the "12-Month Cash Flow" tab.
c0825: Cleaning plan for the kitchen, the trompo and the salsa bar
c0826: Trompo and drip tray, griddle, comal, fryer, hood filters, refrigerated prep table and salsa containers, each with its log.
c0827: Trial services with the full menu
c0829: Run several trial services to tune the marinade, the portion size per taco and the ticket times before opening.
c0832: Walk-in cooler, salsa prep table, hot holding for the guisados, the trompo probe and the cleaning sheet; correct any deviation before you serve.
c0839: Hood and duct cleaning by a certified contractor at the frequency NFPA 96 sets for your type of cooking (solid fuel and high volume need it more often); grease filters as often as your cleaning plan says.
c0840: Fire suppression inspection every 6 months and gas appliance service
c0842: The fire suppression system needs a licensed technician's inspection every 6 months; schedule service of the gas appliances with your licensed contractor too. Write the dates on the calendar.
c0843: Measure the trompo yield and recalculate
c0845: Weigh the raw cone and the leftover at closing every day, log both on your daily production sheet, and take the average to the Taco Cost & Trompo Yield Calculator: measure in the calculator, recalculate in the plan.
c0846: Schedule for Saturday night and the peak dates
c0848: May is the peak of the year (Cinco de Mayo and the patio), and Mexican Independence Day and Day of the Dead bring their own rushes: plan the schedule and the stock ahead of time.
c0851: Sales, commission, promotions and packaging: if the marketplace share of your sales passes the ceiling you set, or its margin no longer covers the commission, trim the menu there or raise prices. Own drivers only as W-2 employees and only when the volume pays for them.
c0853: Covers per day, average check, cost of goods and labor against the P&L in the Excel; review the taco costing whenever the price of meat, tortillas or avocado changes.
c0855: January and February are the slowest months and coincide with the launch: look at the balance of each month before a big payment.
